strengths: Pioneers a highly novel direction of using 2D Gaussian Splatting (2DGS) as a machine-native, spatially adaptive, and compact visual substrate for vision-language pre-training.

Provides excellent systems and algorithmic optimizations, including specialized batched CUDA kernels (achieving over 90× speedup), structured initialization, and luminance-aware pruning, making large-scale 2DGS processing viable.
Presents a well-designed adaptation framework (GS Stem and Perceiver Resampler) that successfully leverages frozen RGB-pretrained ViT backbones with minimal trainable parameters (only ~7%).
Evaluates on a large-scale setup using a 12.8M subset of DataComp, showing promising zero-shot ImageNet performance (13-15%) alongside high input compression (3-20×).
weaknesses: There is still an absolute performance gap of 3.5-5.5% in zero-shot top-1 accuracy on ImageNet-1K compared to the RGB teacher model.

The paper lacks a direct, rigorous baseline comparison against standard compressed formats (such as JPEG/WebP) at equivalent file sizes or bitrates. It would be highly informative to see if a heavily compressed JPEG sent to a standard CLIP model performs better or worse than the proposed 2DGS pipeline.

While 2DGS reduces transmission energy, the local computational cost of fitting 2DGS on resource-constrained edge devices is not quantitatively evaluated. An end-to-end energy/latency analysis comparing 'local 2DGS fitting + transmission' vs. 'JPEG compression + transmission' is crucial to support the edge-cloud deployment claims.

strengths: Highly original and creative paradigm shift: exploring 2D Gaussian Splatting (2DGS) as a direct, compact visual substrate for multimodal vision-language alignment (CLIP) instead of traditional dense pixel grids.

Impressive system-level engineering contributions: developing batched CUDA kernels, structured grid-based initialization, and L1/luminance pruning, which collectively yield a ~90x speedup in fitting time and ~97% GPU utilization compared to prior implementations.

Well-designed architectural adaptation (GS Stem and Perceiver Resampler) to process variable-length, unordered sets of Gaussians into fixed-size visual tokens compatible with frozen pretrained vision transformers.

Honest and thorough experimental analysis on a large-scale dataset (12.8M DataComp subset), including comparisons of parameter-efficient adaptation versus training from scratch, showing the viability of the representation.
weaknesses: Lack of a complete edge-compute vs. transmission trade-off analysis. While the paper motivates 2DGS by reducing edge-to-cloud transmission energy, performing 2DGS optimization (e.g., 3000 iterations) on a resource-constrained edge device requires substantial compute. The paper should discuss or estimate whether this local compute energy overhead offsets the communication savings.

Comparison against standard compression codecs is missing. The reported 3-23.5x compression ratios are compared to raw pixels. In real-world edge-cloud systems, images are transmitted using codecs like JPEG or WebP, which also compress data heavily. It is unclear how 2DGS compares to standard JPEG-compressed inputs in terms of the rate-distortion-accuracy trade-off.

Performance gap on absolute scales: The zero-shot ImageNet accuracy of the adapted 2DGS model (13-15%) still lags behind the RGB teacher (18.5%). Since the teacher itself is trained in a low-accuracy regime (using a reduced-width ViT on a data subset), it remains uncertain if the performance gap will scale favorably or widen when moving to full-scale, high-performing foundation models.

strengths: Innovative and original concept: Exploring 2D Gaussian Splatting (2DGS) as a continuous, spatially adaptive alternative to rigid patch-based visual tokens for vision-language models is highly creative.

Solid engineering and system optimizations: The development of batched CUDA kernels, structured initialization, and L1 regularization-based pruning achieves an impressive ~90× speedup, making large-scale 2DGS fitting practical.

Thoughtful adapter design: The proposed GS Stem (utilizing Fourier positional encodings, log-scaled covariances, gated activations, and a Perceiver Resampler) successfully bridges the unstructured Gaussian parameters with standard frozen Transformer backbones.
weaknesses: Contradiction in edge-cloud motivation: The paper argues that transmitting RGB images from edge devices is energy-intensive. However, generating 2DGS representations requires running an iterative optimization (fitting) process. Running gradient-based optimization on an edge device would consume orders of magnitude more energy and compute than standard, hardware-accelerated JPEG/WebP compression and transmission. A comparative analysis of this trade-off is missing.

Low baseline performance: The RGB teacher model trained on the 12.8M DataComp subset only achieves 18.5% top-1 accuracy on ImageNet-1K, whereas standard OpenCLIP baselines on DataComp-medium (12.8M) typically exceed 50%. This weak baseline makes it difficult to assess how well the proposed approach scales to competitive regimes.

Limited evaluation suite: Despite heavily motivating the work with Visual Language Models (VLMs) and LLM token constraints, the evaluation is restricted to zero-shot ImageNet-1K classification. Standard VLM benchmarks (VQA, captioning, etc.) are not explored.

Dependency on RGB pre-training: As shown in Figure 7, training 2DGS encoders from scratch performs poorly compared to transferring from an RGB teacher. This indicates that the 2DGS representation currently cannot stand on its own and still requires a pre-trained pixel-based model.

strengths: A highly original and timely exploration of 2D Gaussian Splatting (2DGS) as a direct, compressed input modality for large-scale multimodal vision-language alignment (CLIP).
Strong engineering and system-level contributions, including batched and optimized CUDA kernels that achieve a 90x speedup over prior implementations, enabling the processing of millions of images.

Principled algorithmic enhancements to 2DGS fitting, specifically the structured grid-based initialization and the luminance-aware L1 pruning strategy, which dramatically improve both reconstruction quality and convergence.
Extensive validation on a large-scale dataset (12.8M DataComp images) across a comprehensive benchmark of 38 diverse datasets.
Excellent and thorough ablation studies in the appendix detailing alternative architectures (e.g., Point Transformers), normalization strategies, and training recipes.
weaknesses: Missing edge energy/computation trade-off analysis: The paper motivates the use of 2DGS by pointing out the high transmission energy costs of raw RGB images from edge to cloud. However, fitting 2DGS to an image requires an iterative optimization process (e.g., 2000 iterations). Running this local optimization on a resource-constrained edge device likely consumes significantly more energy than standard hardware-accelerated JPEG compression and transmission. A quantitative analysis comparing the local compute energy of 2DGS fitting versus transmission energy is necessary to fully support the motivation.

Heavy reliance on a pretrained RGB teacher: The two-stage training scheme requires distillation from a pretrained RGB ViT to converge successfully, as training from scratch on GS inputs yields poor results. This limits the perspective of 2DGS being a standalone visual substrate, as it currently functions more as a compressed derivative of pixel-based representations.

strengths: Conceptual Novelty: The paper explores a highly interesting and non-trivial paradigm shift—using 2D Gaussian Splatting (2DGS) as a native visual representation for large-scale multimodal learning instead of standard pixel patches. This directly addresses token explosion and transmission overhead from a representation-first perspective.

Solid System Engineering: To make processing feasible on a 12.8M image dataset (DataComp), the authors designed custom batched CUDA kernels, structured grid-based initialization, and luminance-aware pruning. These optimizations achieve an impressive 90x speedup in image fitting compared to prior codebases.

Comprehensive Evaluation: The method is validated on a large-scale setup across 38 diverse datasets from the CLIP benchmark. The results show that the 2DGS representation can preserve 91-98% of the baseline RGB performance while compressing the representation sizes by 3x to 23.5x.

Extensive Ablation Studies: The appendix provides thoroughly detailed analyses and ablations of alternative architectures (such as Point Transformers vs. Perceiver), distillation losses, and normalization strategies, making the findings highly reproducible and valuable for the community.
weaknesses: Dependence on Teacher Model: Direct training from scratch on 2DGS inputs converges poorly, requiring a two-stage training scheme that heavily relies on a pre-trained RGB teacher model. This suggests that native inductive biases for GS-based architectures are still a major open challenge, and performance remains upper-bounded by the teacher.

Comparison to Standard Compressed Formats: While the paper compares 2DGS against uncompressed raw RGB pixels (showing 3x-23.5x compression), modern pipelines transmit images compressed with standard codecs like JPEG. A comparison of 2DGS file sizes/bitrates against equivalent JPEG compression levels (at matching zero-shot accuracies) would provide a more complete picture of its practical edge-to-cloud transmission benefits.

Absolute Performance Scale: The absolute accuracy of the baseline model is somewhat low (22.2% average accuracy), which is understandable given the academically practical 38M model size (ViT-B/16 Small) and the 12.8M pretraining set. It remains to be verified how well these findings and the distillation process scale to larger model capacities (e.g., standard ViT-B or ViT-L).

strengths: Explores a highly original and timely research direction: replacing dense pixel representations with 2D Gaussian Splatting as a compact, machine-friendly visual substrate for vision-language models.

Significant system-level contributions, including batched CUDA kernels, grid-based structured initialization, and luminance pruning, achieving an impressive 90x speedup and 97% GPU utilization compared to prior 2DGS baselines.

Evaluated on a large scale (12.8M DataComp image-text pairs) across a diverse set of 38 zero-shot benchmarks, demonstrating that 2DGS can retain 90-98% of the baseline model's accuracy while compressing inputs.
Excellent diagnostic analysis and comprehensive ablations including distillation strategies, loss functions, token counts, and normalization choices.
weaknesses: Conceptual mismatch in the edge-cloud motivation: The authors argue that transmitting dense RGB images is energy-intensive for edge devices. However, running the iterative 2DGS fitting process on a resource-constrained edge device is likely far more compute- and energy-intensive than simple JPEG compression, which is heavily hardware-accelerated. The paper lacks a concrete analysis of the local computation cost on edge devices.

Strong dependency on pre-trained RGB teachers: The proposed two-stage training relies heavily on distillation from a pre-trained RGB ViT model. Training from scratch yields poor performance (as shown in Figure 15/21), meaning 2DGS is not yet a standalone visual substrate but rather a derivative of pixel-space pre-training.

Low absolute performance: The baseline used, 'ViT-B/16 (Small)', has a low absolute average accuracy of 22.20% across the 38 benchmarks. Consequently, while the relative performance of the GS variants is high (90-98% of baseline), the absolute accuracy remains low, making it difficult to judge the true scalability to state-of-the-art, full-sized CLIP models.
